title: The fly in the honey
hookLine: a fly lands on a pot of honey to sip, and finds its feet stuck
carry: do the work, offer the fruit

cards: A fly finds a pot of honey. What luck. It lands on the rim, walks down to the sweet part, and starts to drink.

A minute later it tries to lift off, and can't. Its feet are stuck in the very thing it came to enjoy. Vivekananda uses a picture like this in his talks on Karma Yoga, and it isn't really about flies.
It's about a new job, a relationship, a project, a phone.

teach.h: WE CAME TO WORK; WE'RE BEING WORKED.
teach.b: His diagnosis comes in a run of short reversals. We came to enjoy, and we're being enjoyed. We came to rule, and we're being ruled.
We came to work, and we're being worked. The honey isn't the problem. Work isn't the problem either; again and again he tells people to work.
The trouble is the sticking: work done for what it will get us, so that the getting owns us. So how do you drink without getting stuck?
Not by staying away from the honey. Running from the world doesn't free anyone. The answer he calls non-attachment, and he offers two roads to it, for two kinds of people.

teach.h: THE GITA: THE WORK, NOT THE FRUITS.
teach.b: If you believe in God, there's the road of the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna tells Arjuna: your right is to the work, never to its fruits. Hindus call it nishkama karma, action without craving.
Work, and give the results away to God, the way you'd lay a flower at a shrine. The work is yours to do. What comes of it isn't yours to clutch.
And if you don't believe in God, he doesn't send you away.
He offers the road of reflection and will: keep telling yourself, this outcome is not me, this praise is not me, this failure is not me, until it's true. The fly can still drink.
It just learns to keep its feet on the rim.

how: Hindus who follow the Bhagavad Gita's teaching on work describe offering their work to God without clinging to its results, and Vedanta study circles read Vivekananda's Karma Yoga alongside the Gita.

o: a habit of working fast so the day ends sooner
a rule to work only on the tasks you enjoy
the yoga of work, without getting stuck in its rewards

games.q: the honey and the fly — tap the pairs.
p: the work we came to enjoy
work done for what it gets us
the Gita: offer the fruits to God
tell yourself: this is not me

s: Vivekananda told people to stay away from the honey and quit work
running from the world frees no one; he wanted hard work without the sticking.
he offered a road to non-attachment for people who don't believe in God
reflection and will: this outcome is not me.
in his reversals, we came to rule and end up ruled
we came to work, and we're being worked.

games.q: you're the fly, and your feet are stuck in the honey you came to enjoy. what does the yoga of work tell you to do?
o: keep drinking, but learn not to sink your feet in.
games.why: Vivekananda's answer isn't to leave the world. it's non-attachment: do the work fully, and let the results go, by offering them to God or by seeing they aren't you.

practice: Name one thing you're working on that you care about a lot, and notice where your feet are stuck: a result you need, someone's approval, a number.

If you pray, picture setting that result down at a shrine and leaving it there; if you don't, say silently on each out-breath, this result is not me. Either way, keep caring about the work, and just lift one foot off the honey.

wordCard.voice: Karma Yoga. The yoga of work: doing the work and offering the fruit, drinking the honey without getting stuck in it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: non-attachment, not being stuck to the results.

carryVoice: Your line: do the work, offer the fruit. Keep your feet on the rim. Tomorrow, a king, a fawn, and the small things we do every day. Day nine hundred forty-three.

sources.ref: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, the chapters on the secret of work and on non-attachment
